Let $\Theta$ be a parameter space and, for each $\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta$, let $\mathbb P_{\boldsymbol\theta}$ denote a probability measure.
This note collects notation and auxiliary results for asymptotic statements that hold uniformly over the family $\mathcal P=\{\mathbb P_{\boldsymbol\theta}:\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta\}$.

# Stochastic Order

We first define notation for uniform convergence in probability.
We say $\boldsymbol X_n \in \mathbb{R}^k$ converges in $\mathcal{P}$ to $\boldsymbol X \in \mathbb{R}^k$, written as $\boldsymbol X_n \stackrel{\mathcal{P}}{\to} \boldsymbol X$, if for every $\epsilon > 0$,
$$
\lim_{n \to \infty} \sup_{\boldsymbol\theta \in \Theta} \mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\|\boldsymbol X_n - \boldsymbol X\| > \epsilon) = 0.
$$
For a positive deterministic sequence $r_n$, we write $\boldsymbol X_n=o_{\mathcal{P}}(r_n)$ if $\boldsymbol X_n/r_n \stackrel{\mathcal{P}}{\to} \boldsymbol 0$.
We write $\boldsymbol X_n=O_{\mathcal{P}}(r_n)$ if, for every $\epsilon > 0$, there exist finite constants $m$ and $n_0$ such that
$$
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta}\left(\|\boldsymbol X_n\|>mr_n\right)
<\epsilon
$$
for all $n\geq n_0$.
The next proposition collects useful stochastic-order relationships:

::: {#prp-stochastic-order}
Let $X_n$ and $Y_n$ be real-valued random variables, and let $r_n$ and $s_n$ be positive deterministic sequences.
Then:

[(i)]{.part-label} $X_n=O_{\mathcal{P}}(r_n),\ Y_n=O_{\mathcal{P}}(s_n) \quad\Rightarrow\quad X_n+Y_n=O_{\mathcal{P}}(r_n+s_n)$.

[(ii)]{.part-label} $X_n=O_{\mathcal{P}}(r_n),\ Y_n=O_{\mathcal{P}}(s_n) \quad\Rightarrow\quad X_nY_n=O_{\mathcal{P}}(r_ns_n)$.

[(iii)]{.part-label} $X_n=o_{\mathcal{P}}(r_n),\ Y_n=O_{\mathcal{P}}(s_n) \quad\Rightarrow\quad X_nY_n=o_{\mathcal{P}}(r_ns_n)$.

[(iv)]{.part-label} $X_n=O_{\mathcal{P}}(r_n),\ r_n\to 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad X_n=o_{\mathcal{P}}(1)$.
:::

::: {.proof-block}
*Proof.*
For $m>0$, write $A_n^m=\{|X_n|>mr_n\}$ and $B_n^m=\{|Y_n|>ms_n\}$.

[(i)]{.part-label} Fix $\epsilon>0$.
By the two stochastic-order assumptions, we can choose finite constants $m_X$ and $m_Y$ and an index $n_0$ so that

$$
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta}\left(A_n^{m_X}\right)<\epsilon/2,
\qquad
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta}\left(B_n^{m_Y}\right)<\epsilon/2
$$

for all $n\geq n_0$.
Taking $m=\max\{m_X,m_Y\}$, the same bounds hold with $m$ in place of $m_X$ and $m_Y$.
On $\left(A_n^{m}\right)^c\cap\left(B_n^{m}\right)^c$ we have $|X_n+Y_n|\leq|X_n|+|Y_n|\leq m(r_n+s_n)$, so

$$
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta}\bigl(|X_n+Y_n|>m(r_n+s_n)\bigr)
\leq
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta}\left(A_n^{m}\right)
+
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta}\left(B_n^{m}\right)
<\epsilon
$$

for $n\geq n_0$.
Hence $X_n+Y_n=O_{\mathcal{P}}(r_n+s_n)$.

[(ii)]{.part-label} With the same $m$ and $n_0$, on $\left(A_n^{m}\right)^c\cap\left(B_n^{m}\right)^c$ we have $|X_nY_n|\leq|X_n|\,|Y_n|\leq m^2 r_ns_n$, so $\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(|X_nY_n|>m^2 r_ns_n)<\epsilon$ for $n\geq n_0$.
Hence $X_nY_n=O_{\mathcal{P}}(r_ns_n)$.

[(iii)]{.part-label} Suppose $X_n=o_{\mathcal{P}}(r_n)$, and fix $\epsilon>0$ and $\delta>0$.
Since $Y_n=O_{\mathcal{P}}(s_n)$, we can choose $m$ and $n_0$ such that

$$
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta}\left(B_n^{m}\right)<\delta
$$

for all $n\geq n_0$.
On $\left(B_n^{m}\right)^c$, the event $|X_nY_n|>\epsilon r_ns_n$ implies $|X_n|>(\epsilon/m)r_n$, so

$$
\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(|X_nY_n|>\epsilon r_ns_n)
\leq
\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta}\bigl(|X_n|>(\epsilon/m)r_n\bigr)
+\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta}\left(B_n^{m}\right).
$$

Taking the supremum over $\boldsymbol\theta$ and the limit superior gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
&\limsup_{n\to\infty}
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(|X_nY_n|>\epsilon r_ns_n) \\
&\qquad\leq
\limsup_{n\to\infty}
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta}\bigl(|X_n|>(\epsilon/m)r_n\bigr)
+
\limsup_{n\to\infty}
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta}\left(B_n^{m}\right)
\leq \delta.
\end{aligned}
$$

Taking $\delta\downarrow0$, we can conclude $X_nY_n=o_{\mathcal{P}}(r_ns_n)$.

[(iv)]{.part-label} Suppose $X_n=O_{\mathcal{P}}(r_n)$ with $r_n\to 0$, and fix $\delta>0$ and $\epsilon>0$.
Choose $m$ and $n_0$ with $\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta}\left(A_n^{m}\right)<\epsilon$ for $n\geq n_0$.
Since $r_n\to 0$, there is $n_1$ with $mr_n<\delta$ for $n\geq n_1$.
Therefore $\{|X_n|>\delta\}\subseteq A_n^{m}$ and $\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(|X_n|>\delta)<\epsilon$ for $n\geq\max(n_0,n_1)$.
Since $\epsilon>0$ was arbitrary, $X_n=o_{\mathcal{P}}(1)$.
$\square$
:::

The next proposition converts uniform moment bounds into stochastic-order statements.

::: {#prp-uniform-moment-bounds}
Let $\boldsymbol X_n$ be a random vector, let $r_n$ be a positive deterministic sequence, and fix $q>0$.

[(i)]{.part-label} If

$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}
\left[
\left(\frac{\|\boldsymbol X_n\|}{r_n}\right)^q
\right]
=0,
$$

then $\boldsymbol X_n=o_{\mathcal P}(r_n)$.

[(ii)]{.part-label} If

$$
\limsup_{n\to\infty}
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}
\left[
\left(\frac{\|\boldsymbol X_n\|}{r_n}\right)^q
\right]
<\infty,
$$

then $\boldsymbol X_n=O_{\mathcal P}(r_n)$.
:::

::: {.proof-block}
*Proof.*
For every $m>0$, Markov's inequality gives

$$
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\mathbb P_{\boldsymbol\theta}\left(\|\boldsymbol X_n\|>mr_n\right)
\leq
\frac{1}{m^q}
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}
\left[
\left(\frac{\|\boldsymbol X_n\|}{r_n}\right)^q
\right].
$$

Under the condition in part (i), take $m=\epsilon$ for arbitrary $\epsilon>0$.
The right-hand side converges to zero, so $\boldsymbol X_n/r_n\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\to}\boldsymbol0$.

Under the condition in part (ii), there exist finite $c$ and $n_0$ such that

$$
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}
\left[
\left(\frac{\|\boldsymbol X_n\|}{r_n}\right)^q
\right]
\leq c
$$
for every $n\geq n_0$.
For any $\epsilon>0$, choosing $m>(c/\epsilon)^{1/q}$ makes the preceding probability strictly smaller than $\epsilon$ for every $n\geq n_0$.
Hence $\boldsymbol X_n=O_{\mathcal P}(r_n)$.
$\square$
:::

# Asymptotic Equivalence

For each positive integer $q$, define the class of functions
$$
\mathcal G_q
=
\left\{
g:\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R:
|g(\boldsymbol x)|\leq1,
|g(\boldsymbol x)-g(\boldsymbol y)|\leq\|\boldsymbol x-\boldsymbol y\|
\quad\text{for all }\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y\in\mathbb R^q
\right\}.
$$
When the dimension is clear, we write $\mathcal G$ for $\mathcal G_q$.
For $\boldsymbol X_n,\boldsymbol Z_n\in\mathbb R^q$, we say $\boldsymbol X_n$ is asymptotically equivalent in $\mathcal{P}$ to $\boldsymbol Z_n$, written $\boldsymbol X_n\stackrel{\mathcal{P}}{\approx}\boldsymbol Z_n$, if
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\sup_{g\in\mathcal G_q}
\left|
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta}[g(\boldsymbol X_n)]
-
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta}[g(\boldsymbol Z_n)]
\right|
=0.
$$

The next proposition shows that asymptotic equivalence preserves uniform stochastic boundedness:

::: {#prp-asymptotic-equivalence-tightness}
If $\boldsymbol X_n\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\approx}\boldsymbol Z_n$, then
$$
\boldsymbol X_n=O_{\mathcal P}(1)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\boldsymbol Z_n=O_{\mathcal P}(1).
$$
:::

::: {.proof-block}
*Proof.*
Suppose $\boldsymbol Z_n=O_{\mathcal P}(1)$.
For $m>1$, define
$$
g_m(\boldsymbol x)
=
\min\left\{1,(\|\boldsymbol x\|-m+1)_+\right\}.
$$
The function $g_m$ belongs to $\mathcal G_q$ and satisfies
$$
\mathbb 1\{\|\boldsymbol x\|>m\}
\leq
g_m(\boldsymbol x)
\leq
\mathbb 1\{\|\boldsymbol x\|>m-1\}.
$$
Therefore,
$$
\begin{aligned}
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\mathbb P_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\|\boldsymbol X_n\|>m)
&\leq
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[g_m(\boldsymbol X_n)] \\
&\leq
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[g_m(\boldsymbol Z_n)]
+
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\sup_{g\in\mathcal G_q}
\left|
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[g(\boldsymbol X_n)]
-
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[g(\boldsymbol Z_n)]
\right| \\
&\leq
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\mathbb P_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\|\boldsymbol Z_n\|>m-1)
+\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\sup_{g\in\mathcal G_q}
\left|
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[g(\boldsymbol X_n)]
-
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta}[g(\boldsymbol Z_n)]
\right|.
\end{aligned}
$$
Given $\epsilon>0$, uniform stochastic boundedness of $\boldsymbol Z_n$ allows us to pick a finite $m>1$ so that the first term on the final line is eventually smaller than $\epsilon/2$.
Asymptotic equivalence makes the second term eventually smaller than $\epsilon/2$.
Hence $\boldsymbol X_n=O_{\mathcal P}(1)$.
The reverse implication follows by interchanging $\boldsymbol X_n$ and $\boldsymbol Z_n$.
$\square$
:::

The next proposition connects asymptotic equivalence and convergence to a fixed distribution:

::: {#prp-asymptotic-equivalence-cdf-limit}
For any sequences $n_k\to\infty$ and $\boldsymbol\theta_k\in\Theta$ and any fixed distribution function $F$, the following statements hold:

[(i)]{.part-label} If $\boldsymbol X_n\stackrel{\mathcal{P}}{\approx}\boldsymbol Z_n$ and
$$\lim_{k\to\infty}
\left|
\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}(\boldsymbol Z_{n_k}\leq\boldsymbol t)-F(\boldsymbol t)
\right|
=0
\quad\text{for every continuity point $\boldsymbol t$ of $F$},
$$
then
$$
\lim_{k\to\infty}
\left|
\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}(\boldsymbol X_{n_k}\leq\boldsymbol t)-F(\boldsymbol t)
\right|
=0
\quad\text{for every continuity point $\boldsymbol t$ of $F$}.
$$

[(ii)]{.part-label} If
$$
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{k \to \infty}
\left|
\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}(\boldsymbol X_{n_k}\leq\boldsymbol t)-F(\boldsymbol t)
\right|
&=0, \\
\lim_{k \to \infty}
\left|
\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}(\boldsymbol Z_{n_k}\leq\boldsymbol t)-F(\boldsymbol t)
\right|
&=0
\end{aligned}
$$
for every continuity point $\boldsymbol t$ of $F$, then
$$
\lim_{k\to\infty}
\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}
\left|
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}[g(\boldsymbol X_{n_k})]
-
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}[g(\boldsymbol Z_{n_k})]
\right|
=0.
$$

[(iii)]{.part-label} Suppose $\boldsymbol Z_n$ has distribution function $F$ under $\mathbb P_{\boldsymbol\theta}$ for every $n$ and $\boldsymbol\theta$.
Then $\boldsymbol X_n\stackrel{\mathcal{P}}{\approx}\boldsymbol Z_n$ if and only if, for every continuity point $\boldsymbol t\in\mathbb R^q$ of $F$,
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\left|
\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\boldsymbol X_n\leq\boldsymbol t)-F(\boldsymbol t)
\right|
=0.
$$
:::

::: {.proof-block}
*Proof.*

[(i)]{.part-label} The premise says that, under $\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}$, $\boldsymbol Z_{n_k}$ converges weakly to the fixed distribution with distribution function $F$.
By the bounded-Lipschitz characterization of weak convergence, this implies
$$
\lim_{k\to\infty}
\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}
\left|
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}[g(\boldsymbol Z_{n_k})]
-
\int_{\mathbb R^q}g(\boldsymbol z)\,dF(\boldsymbol z)
\right|
=0.
$$
Moreover, for every $k$, the triangle inequality gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}
\left|
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}[g(\boldsymbol X_{n_k})]
-
\int_{\mathbb R^q}g(\boldsymbol z)\,dF(\boldsymbol z)
\right| \\
&\qquad\leq
\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}
\left|
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}[g(\boldsymbol X_{n_k})]
-
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}[g(\boldsymbol Z_{n_k})]
\right|
\\
&\qquad\quad+
\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}
\left|
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}[g(\boldsymbol Z_{n_k})]
-
\int_{\mathbb R^q}g(\boldsymbol z)\,dF(\boldsymbol z)
\right|.
\end{aligned}
$$
The first term on the right tends to zero because $\boldsymbol X_n\stackrel{\mathcal{P}}{\approx}\boldsymbol Z_n$, and the second tends to zero by the preceding display.
Therefore
$$
\lim_{k\to\infty}
\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}
\left|
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}[g(\boldsymbol X_{n_k})]
-
\int_{\mathbb R^q}g(\boldsymbol z)\,dF(\boldsymbol z)
\right|
=0.
$$
Thus $\boldsymbol X_{n_k}$ converges weakly to $F$ under $\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}$.
The claimed convergence of distribution functions at every continuity point of $F$ follows from the portmanteau theorem.

[(ii)]{.part-label} The two premises imply that, under $\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}$, both $\boldsymbol X_{n_k}$ and $\boldsymbol Z_{n_k}$ converge weakly to the fixed distribution with distribution function $F$.
The bounded-Lipschitz characterization of weak convergence therefore gives
$$
\begin{aligned}
\lim_{k\to\infty}
\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}
\left|
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}[g(\boldsymbol X_{n_k})]
-
\int_{\mathbb R^q}g(\boldsymbol z)\,dF(\boldsymbol z)
\right|&=0, \\
\lim_{k\to\infty}
\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}
\left|
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}[g(\boldsymbol Z_{n_k})]
-
\int_{\mathbb R^q}g(\boldsymbol z)\,dF(\boldsymbol z)
\right|&=0.
\end{aligned}
$$
By the triangle inequality,
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}
\left|
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}[g(\boldsymbol X_{n_k})]
-
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}[g(\boldsymbol Z_{n_k})]
\right| \\
&\qquad\leq
\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}
\left|
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}[g(\boldsymbol X_{n_k})]
-
\int_{\mathbb R^q}g(\boldsymbol z)\,dF(\boldsymbol z)
\right| \\
&\qquad\quad+
\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}
\left|
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}[g(\boldsymbol Z_{n_k})]
-
\int_{\mathbb R^q}g(\boldsymbol z)\,dF(\boldsymbol z)
\right|.
\end{aligned}
$$
Both terms on the right tend to zero, so
$$
\lim_{k\to\infty}
\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}
\left|
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}[g(\boldsymbol X_{n_k})]
-
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}[g(\boldsymbol Z_{n_k})]
\right|
=0.
$$

[(iii)]{.part-label} First suppose $\boldsymbol X_n\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\approx}\boldsymbol Z_n$.
If the asserted uniform convergence failed, there would be a continuity point $\boldsymbol t$ of $F$, an $\epsilon>0$, and sequences $n_k\to\infty$ and $\boldsymbol\theta_k\in\Theta$ such that
$$
\left|
\mathbb P_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}(\boldsymbol X_{n_k}\leq\boldsymbol t)
-F(\boldsymbol t)
\right|
\geq\epsilon
$$
for every $k$.
Because $\boldsymbol Z_{n_k}$ has distribution function $F$ under $\mathbb P_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}$, part (i) implies that the left-hand side converges to zero, a contradiction.

Conversely, suppose the asserted uniform convergence holds.
If $\boldsymbol X_n\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\approx}\boldsymbol Z_n$ failed, there would be an $\epsilon>0$ and sequences $n_k\to\infty$ and $\boldsymbol\theta_k\in\Theta$ such that
$$
\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}
\left|
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}[g(\boldsymbol X_{n_k})]
-
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}[g(\boldsymbol Z_{n_k})]
\right|
\geq\epsilon
$$
for every $k$.
The asserted uniform convergence implies that $\boldsymbol X_{n_k}$ converges weakly to $F$ under $\mathbb P_{\boldsymbol\theta_k}$, while $\boldsymbol Z_{n_k}$ has distribution function $F$ for every $k$.
Part (ii) therefore implies that the preceding bounded-Lipschitz distance converges to zero, a contradiction.
$\square$
:::

Part (iii) of @prp-asymptotic-equivalence-cdf-limit implies asymptotic equivalence reduces to uniform weak convergence when the target distribution is fixed.

The next proposition shows that asymptotic equivalence is preserved under uniformly negligible perturbations:

::: {#prp-asymptotic-equivalence-perturbation}
If $\boldsymbol X_n\stackrel{\mathcal{P}}{\approx}\boldsymbol Z_n$ and $\boldsymbol Y_n-\boldsymbol X_n=o_{\mathcal{P}}(1)$, then
$$
\boldsymbol Y_n\stackrel{\mathcal{P}}{\approx}\boldsymbol Z_n.
$$
:::

::: {.proof-block}
*Proof.*
By the triangle inequality, we have
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}
\left|
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta}[g(\boldsymbol Y_n)]-\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta}[g(\boldsymbol Z_n)]
\right| \\
&\qquad\leq
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}
\left|
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta}[g(\boldsymbol Y_n)]-\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta}[g(\boldsymbol X_n)]
\right| \\
&\qquad\quad+
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}
\left|
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta}[g(\boldsymbol X_n)]-\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta}[g(\boldsymbol Z_n)]
\right|.
\end{aligned}
$$
The second term tends to zero because $\boldsymbol X_n\stackrel{\mathcal{P}}{\approx}\boldsymbol Z_n$.
To see that the first term also tends to zero, pick $g\in\mathcal G$ and $\delta>0$.
Then
$$
\begin{aligned}
\left|
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta}[g(\boldsymbol Y_n)]-\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta}[g(\boldsymbol X_n)]
\right|
&\leq
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta}\left|g(\boldsymbol Y_n)-g(\boldsymbol X_n)\right| \\
&\leq
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta}\min\{2,\|\boldsymbol Y_n-\boldsymbol X_n\|\} \\
&\leq
\delta
+
2\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\|\boldsymbol Y_n-\boldsymbol X_n\|>\delta).
\end{aligned}
$$
Taking the supremum over $g\in\mathcal G$ and $\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta$, then the limit superior as $n\to\infty$, gives an upper bound of $\delta$ because $\boldsymbol Y_n-\boldsymbol X_n=o_{\mathcal{P}}(1)$.
Letting $\delta\downarrow0$ shows
$$
\lim_{n\to\infty}
\sup_{\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta}
\sup_{g\in\mathcal G}
\left|
\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta}[g(\boldsymbol Y_n)]-\mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol\theta}[g(\boldsymbol X_n)]
\right|
=0. \qquad\square
$$
:::

# Convergence Tools

The next proposition records continuous mapping results:

::: {#prp-continuous-mapping}

<br>

[(i)]{.part-label} Suppose $\boldsymbol X_n\stackrel{\mathcal{P}}{\to}\boldsymbol X$ and there is a compact set $K\subseteq\mathbb R^k$ such that $\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\boldsymbol X\in K)=1$ for every $\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta$.
If $h:\mathbb R^k\to\mathbb R^m$ is measurable and continuous on an open set containing $K$, then

$$
h(\boldsymbol X_n)\stackrel{\mathcal{P}}{\to}h(\boldsymbol X).
$$

[(ii)]{.part-label} Suppose $\boldsymbol X_n\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\approx}\boldsymbol Z_n$ and $\boldsymbol Z_n=O_{\mathcal P}(1)$.
Let $h:\mathbb R^k\to\mathbb R^m$ be measurable.
If every weak subsequential limit of $\boldsymbol Z_n$ assigns probability zero to the discontinuity set of $h$, then

$$
h(\boldsymbol X_n)
\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\approx}
h(\boldsymbol Z_n).
$$
:::

::: {.proof-block}
*Proof.*

[(i)]{.part-label} Fix $\epsilon>0$.
By compactness of $K$ and continuity of $h$ on a neighborhood of $K$, there exists $\delta>0$ such that

$$
\boldsymbol z\in\mathbb R^k,\ \boldsymbol x\in K,\ \|\boldsymbol z-\boldsymbol x\|<\delta
\quad\Rightarrow\quad
\|h(\boldsymbol z)-h(\boldsymbol x)\|<\epsilon.
$$

Since $\boldsymbol X\in K$ almost surely under every $\mathbb{P}_{\boldsymbol\theta}$,

$$
\left\{
\|h(\boldsymbol X_n)-h(\boldsymbol X)\|>\epsilon
\right\}
\cap
\{\boldsymbol X\in K\}
\subseteq
\left\{
\|\boldsymbol X_n-\boldsymbol X\|>\delta/2
\right\}.
$$

The right-hand side tends to zero because $\boldsymbol X_n\stackrel{\mathcal{P}}{\to}\boldsymbol X$.
Since $\epsilon>0$ was arbitrary, $h(\boldsymbol X_n)\stackrel{\mathcal{P}}{\to}h(\boldsymbol X)$.

[(ii)]{.part-label} Suppose the conclusion fails.
Then there are $\epsilon>0$ and sequences $n_\ell\to\infty$ and $\boldsymbol\theta_\ell\in\Theta$ such that

$$
\sup_{g\in\mathcal G_m}
\left|
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_\ell}[g(h(\boldsymbol X_{n_\ell}))]
-
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_\ell}[g(h(\boldsymbol Z_{n_\ell}))]
\right|
\geq\epsilon
$$

for every $\ell$.
Let $\mu_\ell$ denote the law of $\boldsymbol Z_{n_\ell}$ under $\mathbb P_{\boldsymbol\theta_\ell}$.
The sequence $\{\mu_\ell\}$ is tight.
By Prokhorov's theorem, there is a subsequence $\{\mu_{\ell_j}\}$ that converges weakly to the law of some random vector $\boldsymbol W$ on $\mathbb R^k$.
Part (i) of @prp-asymptotic-equivalence-cdf-limit and $\boldsymbol X_n\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\approx}\boldsymbol Z_n$ imply that $\boldsymbol X_{n_{\ell_j}}$ also converges weakly to $\boldsymbol W$.
By assumption, the law of $\boldsymbol W$ assigns probability zero to the discontinuity set of $h$.
The continuous mapping theorem therefore implies that both $h(\boldsymbol X_{n_{\ell_j}})$ and $h(\boldsymbol Z_{n_{\ell_j}})$ converge weakly to $h(\boldsymbol W)$.
Part (ii) of @prp-asymptotic-equivalence-cdf-limit then gives

$$
\lim_{j\to\infty}
\sup_{g\in\mathcal G_m}
\left|
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_{\ell_j}}[g(h(\boldsymbol X_{n_{\ell_j}}))]
-
\mathbb E_{\boldsymbol\theta_{\ell_j}}[g(h(\boldsymbol Z_{n_{\ell_j}}))]
\right|
=0,
$$

contradicting the preceding lower bound.
Thus $h(\boldsymbol X_n)\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\approx}h(\boldsymbol Z_n)$.
$\square$
:::

The next proposition records a useful joint-convergence rule:

::: {#prp-joint-convergence}
[(i)]{.part-label} If $\boldsymbol X_n\stackrel{\mathcal{P}}{\to}\boldsymbol X$ and $\boldsymbol Y_n\stackrel{\mathcal{P}}{\to}\boldsymbol Y$, then

$$
(\boldsymbol X_n,\boldsymbol Y_n)\stackrel{\mathcal{P}}{\to}(\boldsymbol X,\boldsymbol Y).
$$

[(ii)]{.part-label} If $\boldsymbol X_n\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\approx}\boldsymbol Z_n$ and $\boldsymbol Y_n\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\to}\boldsymbol c$, then

$$
(\boldsymbol X_n,\boldsymbol Y_n)
\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\approx}
(\boldsymbol Z_n,\boldsymbol c).
$$
:::

::: {.proof-block}
*Proof.*
[(i)]{.part-label} Suppose $\boldsymbol X_n\stackrel{\mathcal{P}}{\to}\boldsymbol X$ and $\boldsymbol Y_n\stackrel{\mathcal{P}}{\to}\boldsymbol Y$.
For every $\epsilon>0$,

$$
\left\{
\|(\boldsymbol X_n,\boldsymbol Y_n)-(\boldsymbol X,\boldsymbol Y)\|>\epsilon
\right\}
\subseteq
\left\{
\|\boldsymbol X_n-\boldsymbol X\|>\epsilon/2
\right\}
\cup
\left\{
\|\boldsymbol Y_n-\boldsymbol Y\|>\epsilon/2
\right\}.
$$

Taking probabilities, taking the supremum over $\boldsymbol\theta\in\Theta$, and using the two marginal convergences proves

$$
(\boldsymbol X_n,\boldsymbol Y_n)\stackrel{\mathcal{P}}{\to}(\boldsymbol X,\boldsymbol Y).
$$

[(ii)]{.part-label} For every bounded, 1-Lipschitz function $g$ on the product space, the map $\boldsymbol x\mapsto g(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol c)$ is bounded and 1-Lipschitz.
Hence

$$
(\boldsymbol X_n,\boldsymbol c)
\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\approx}
(\boldsymbol Z_n,\boldsymbol c).
$$

Moreover,

$$
\left\|(\boldsymbol X_n,\boldsymbol Y_n)-(\boldsymbol X_n,\boldsymbol c)\right\|
=
\left\|\boldsymbol Y_n-\boldsymbol c\right\|
=o_{\mathcal P}(1).
$$

The result follows from @prp-asymptotic-equivalence-perturbation.
$\square$
:::

The final result gives a uniform version of Slutsky's theorem:

::: {#prp-asymptotic-equivalence-slutsky}
Suppose $X_n,Y_n,Z_n\in\mathbb R$ and $c\in\mathbb R$.
If $X_n\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\approx}Z_n$, $Z_n=O_{\mathcal P}(1)$, and $Y_n\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\to}c$, then

[(i)]{.part-label} $X_n+Y_n\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\approx}Z_n+c$.

[(ii)]{.part-label} $X_nY_n\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\approx}cZ_n$.

[(iii)]{.part-label} If $c\neq0$, then $X_n/Y_n\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\approx}Z_n/c$.
:::

::: {.proof-block}
*Proof.*
Part (ii) of @prp-joint-convergence gives

$$
(X_n,Y_n)
\stackrel{\mathcal P}{\approx}
(Z_n,c).
$$

Since $(Z_n,c)=O_{\mathcal P}(1)$, part (ii) of @prp-continuous-mapping can be applied to the maps $(x,y)\mapsto x+y$, $(x,y)\mapsto xy$, and, when $c\neq0$, $(x,y)\mapsto x/y$, defined arbitrarily when $y=0$.
This proves the three conclusions.
$\square$
:::
